steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm married filing jointly in Boston MA. W-2 from Riverside Hospital: $84,900. Additional income: $8,900 (graphic design, 2 clients), $920 from Marcus savings account, $320 from Charles Schwab. Home office: 155 sq ft exclusive; I pay $2,100/month for 780 sq ft. Deductions: $4,800 student loan interest (MOHELA, 2016–2020); $1,400 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) have the receipt; $890 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — I can walk through what’s likely deductible, how to treat the home office and the self‑employment income, whether you should itemize, and which federal/state forms you’ll use. I’ll also flag a few clarifying questions so I can give a tighter recommendation or run example calculations.

Summary (quick answers)
- Likely take the standard deduction for 2024 (married filing jointly = $29,200) unless you have substantial additional itemizable items (large mortgage interest, big property tax/SALT payments up to $10k, large medical expenses over 7.5% of AGI). Based on the items you listed, the standard deduction will probably be larger than your itemized total.
- Your $8,900 graphic‑design income is self‑employment income — report on Schedule C, pay self‑employment tax (Schedule SE), and you can deduct business expenses (including a home‑office share of rent/utilities) on Schedule C.
- Home office: you can use either the simplified method ($5/sq ft → 155 × $5 = $775) or the actual‑expense method (your business % × allowable home expenses). With rent $2,100/mo (=$25,200/yr) and a 155/780 = ~19.87% business use, the rent portion alone would be about $25,200 × 19.87% ≈ $5,005 (so the actual method will likely give a larger deduction than the simplified method).
- Student loan interest: the maximum federal student‑loan interest deduction is $2,500 (above‑the‑line) and phases out at higher MAGI levels — you cannot deduct the full $4,800 if you exceed limits; provide your MAGI if you want a precise determination.
- Charitable donation of $1,400 is deductible only if you itemize.
- Unreimbursed employee expenses for W‑2 work are generally NOT deductible (suspended through 2025). If the $890 in unreimbursed expenses are business expenses for your graphic‑design work, they are deductible on Schedule C.

What to report and where (forms)
- Federal:
  - Form 1040 — main return.
  - Schedule 1 (Form 1040) — for adjustments to income (e.g., half of self‑employment tax is an adjustment) and some other income items.
  - Schedule C — report the $8,900 self‑employment revenue and any business expenses (equipment, supplies, business portion of rent/utilities if you use the actual home‑office method, advertising, software, etc.).
  - Schedule SE — compute self‑employment tax (Social Security + Medicare). You may deduct half of the SE tax as an adjustment on Schedule 1.
  - Form 8829 — if you use the actual method for business use of home, use Form 8829 to compute the allowable home‑office deduction and transfer the result to Schedule C. If you use the simplified method, you do not use Form 8829 — enter the simplified home‑office deduction on Schedule C.
  - Form 8995 or 8995-A — for the Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction (20% of qualified business income) if you qualify. With relatively small net self‑employment income, you’ll likely be eligible for some or all of this deduction; it’s calculated after your Schedule C net income and affects taxable income.
  - Keep/will need 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC if issued by clients (self‑employment income reporting), 1099‑INT (Marcus $920), 1099‑DIV/1099‑INT (Schwab $320), and your W‑2 from Riverside Hospital.
- Massachusetts state tax:
  - MA Form 1 (resident return). MA treats some items differently (e.g., different standard deduction/exemption rules), and interest/dividends are taxed. You’ll report W‑2, self‑employment income and relevant adjustments on the MA return. Expect to pay MA income tax on taxable income (check MA rates and any allowable deductions/credits).

Detailed notes, calculations & tax effects
- Interest income: $920 (Marcus) and $320 (Schwab) are taxable as interest/dividends — reportable on 1040 (and MA return).
- Self‑employment tax and deductible portion:
  - SE tax is ~15.3% on net self‑employment earnings (after business expenses). You then deduct half of the SE tax on Schedule 1 as an adjustment to income.
- Home office choice:
  - Simplified: 155 sq ft × $5 = $775 deduction (easy, no Form 8829).
  - Actual: business percentage = 155 / 780 ≈ 19.87%. Rent $25,200 × 19.87% ≈ $5,005. If you also allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, internet portion, etc., the deduction will be larger. If you own the home, actual method also includes depreciation and requires Form 8829.
  - If the home office is for your self‑employment graphic design, the home‑office deduction reduces Schedule C net income. If the office is instead for your W‑2 job, you cannot use the home‑office deduction (employee business expense deduction is suspended).
- Student loan interest:
  - The deduction is an above‑the‑line deduction (Schedule 1) up to $2,500 (subject to phase‑outs). You do not need to itemize to claim it.
  - You’ll need Form 1098‑E from MOHELA showing interest paid during the tax year. If you actually paid $4,800 in interest in the tax year, the deductible portion is capped at $2,500 (and may be reduced if your MAGI is in the phaseout range).
- Charitable gift $1,400:
  - Deductible only if you itemize; you must keep the receipt. For cash gifts, bank record/receipt is fine.
- Unreimbursed expenses $890:
  - If these are for your W‑2 hospital job, they are not deductible.
  - If they are legitimately business expenses for your self‑employment (tools, software, supplies, mileage, etc.), include them on Schedule C.

Will you benefit from itemizing?
- Quick check of the likely itemizable items you listed:
  - Charity: $1,400
  - Student loan interest: not an itemized deduction (above the line)
  - SALT (state & local tax + property tax): you didn’t list amounts; SALT limit is $10,000
  - Mortgage interest/property tax: none listed (you pay rent)
  - Medical expenses: only deductible to the extent >7.5% of AGI
  - Result: With only $1,400 in charitable gifts and no mortgage interest or large SALT or large medical expenses, itemizing will likely be far less than the 2024 standard deduction ($29,200). So most likely choose the standard deduction.
- If you want I can compute a precise comparison — I’d need any of the following: state tax withheld or state/local taxes paid, mortgage interest or property tax, large medical expenses, or other deductible items.

Practical next steps / what I need from you if you want a concrete calculation
1. Confirm whether the $4,800 student loan interest was paid in the tax year you’re filing for, and whether that amount is the total interest paid (you should have a 1098‑E from MOHELA).
2. Tell me whether the $890 unreimbursed expenses relate to your W‑2 job (hospital) or to your graphic‑design clients.
3. Tell me if you paid any mortgage interest or property taxes, and the amount of state/local taxes paid or withheld (or provide your W‑2 Box 17 state tax withheld).
4. Provide the exact amounts of any 1099s or year‑end statements (interest/dividend 1099s) and federal tax withheld on your W‑2 (Box 2), if you want an estimate of total tax due/refund.
5. Let me know whether you want me to run a sample tax calculation showing:
   - net Schedule C income under both home‑office methods,
   - estimated self‑employment tax,
   - effect on AGI and taxable income,
   - whether the QBI deduction applies,
   - and whether itemizing beats the standard deduction.

Recordkeeping reminders
- Keep receipts and documentation: MOHELA 1098‑E for student interest, donation receipt for Northwest Harvest, documentation of the home office (floorplan or measurement notes, lease showing rent, utility bills), business receipts/invoices and mileage records, and 1099s/1098s/W‑2.
- If you expect to owe extra federal tax because of self‑employment income, you may need to make estimated tax payments (quarterly) to avoid underpayment penalties.

If you want, I can:
- Run a rough tax calculation now using reasonable assumptions (I can show both simplified and actual home‑office scenarios), or
- Draft a checklist email you can send to your tax preparer with the items and forms they’ll need.

Which would you prefer?
